pairs.source_text: Ante mare et terras et quod tegit omnia caelum unus erat toto naturae vultus in orbe, quem dixere chaos: rudis indigestaque moles nec quicquam nisi pondus iners congestaque eodem non bene iunctarum discordia semina rerum.
pairs.question: Quo nomine, ut narrat Ovidius in primo Metamorphoseon libro, appellabatur ille unus naturae vultus, rudis indigestaque moles, ante mare et terras et caelum?
pairs.question_en: By what name, as Ovid tells in the first book of the Metamorphoses, was that single face of nature called — a rough and unordered mass — before sea and lands and sky existed?
pairs.derivation: The opening cosmogonic fact of the Metamorphoses: the primordial state was named Chaos (quem dixere chaos). Anchored to Ovid + Metamorphoses book 1; one-name answer supported verbatim; canonical shared myth every Latin reader carries.

pairs.source_text: Hanc deus et melior litem natura diremit.
pairs.question: Quis apud Ovidium litem elementorum in chao inter se pugnantium diremit mundumque ordinavit?
pairs.question_en: Who, in Ovid, resolved the strife of the elements fighting with one another in chaos and set the world in order?
pairs.derivation: The famous phrase 'deus et melior natura' (1.21) names the orderer of chaos — one of the most quoted lines of the cosmogony. Anchored to Ovid's chaos; short answer verbatim in the source.

pairs.source_text: quam satus Iapeto, mixtam pluvialibus undis, finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta deorum
pairs.question: Quis, ut tradit Ovidius, hominem e terra pluvialibus undis mixta in effigiem deorum finxit?
pairs.question_en: Who, as Ovid relates, fashioned man from earth mixed with rainwater in the image of the gods?
pairs.derivation: Ovid credits the making of man to 'satus Iapeto' — the son of Iapetus, i.e. Prometheus, a standard identification every reader carries. Anchored to Ovid + the creation of man; single-name answer supported by the quoted line.

pairs.source_text: Aurea prima sata est aetas, quae vindice nullo, sponte sua, sine lege fidem rectumque colebat.
pairs.question: Quae aetas hominum apud Ovidium prima fuit, quae sine lege ac vindice sponte sua fidem rectumque colebat?
pairs.question_en: Which age of mankind in Ovid came first, cultivating faith and right of its own accord, without law or enforcer?
pairs.derivation: The golden age as first of the ages, needing no laws — the canonical myth of the ages (1.89-90). Anchored to Ovid's scheme of the ages; short noun-phrase answer verbatim (Aurea prima sata est aetas).

pairs.source_text: ver erat aeternum, placidique tepentibus auris mulcebant zephyri natos sine semine flores;
pairs.question: Quod anni tempus aetate aurea, ut canit Ovidius, aeternum erat?
pairs.question_en: Which season of the year, as Ovid sings, was everlasting in the golden age?
pairs.derivation: 'Ver erat aeternum' — the eternal spring of the golden age, a proverbial feature of the myth. Anchored to the golden age in Ovid; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Postquam Saturno tenebrosa in Tartara misso sub Iove mundus erat, subiit argentea proles, auro deterior, fulvo pretiosior aere.
pairs.question: Quae proles hominum apud Ovidium successit, postquam Saturno in Tartara misso mundus sub Iove erat?
pairs.question_en: Which race of men in Ovid followed, after Saturn was sent to Tartarus and the world came under Jove?
pairs.derivation: The succession of the ages: the golden age belongs to Saturn, and when Jove takes the world the silver race follows. Anchored to Saturn/Jove; short answer verbatim (subiit argentea proles).

pairs.source_text: Iuppiter antiqui contraxit tempora veris perque hiemes aestusque et inaequalis autumnos et breve ver spatiis exegit quattuor annum.
pairs.question: Quis deus, ut narrat Ovidius, antiqui veris tempora contraxit et annum quattuor spatiis primum distinxit?
pairs.question_en: Which god, as Ovid tells, shortened the ancient spring and first divided the year into four seasons?
pairs.derivation: Jupiter ends the eternal spring and institutes the four seasons at the start of the silver age — a canonical aetiology within the ages myth. Anchored to the seasons + Ovid; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tertia post illam successit aenea proles, saevior ingeniis et ad horrida promptior arma, non scelerata tamen; de duro est ultima ferro.
pairs.question: Ex quo metallo ultima hominum aetas apud Ovidium nomen ducit?
pairs.question_en: From which metal does the last age of mankind in Ovid take its name?
pairs.derivation: 'De duro est ultima ferro' — the iron age as the last and worst of the four. Anchored to Ovid's ages; one-word metal answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: victa iacet pietas, et virgo caede madentis ultima caelestum terras Astraea reliquit.
pairs.question: Quae virgo caelestis, ut narrat Ovidius, ultima deorum terras aetate ferrea reliquit?
pairs.question_en: Which celestial maiden, as Ovid tells, was the last of the gods to abandon the earth in the age of iron?
pairs.derivation: Astraea (Justice) as the last divinity to leave the blood-soaked earth of the iron age — a celebrated mythological fact, later tied to the constellation Virgo. Anchored to the iron age + Ovid; single-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: obruta mole sua cum corpora dira iacerent, perfusam multo natorum sanguine Terram immaduisse ferunt calidumque animasse cruorem et, ne nulla suae stirpis monimenta manerent, in faciem vertisse hominum;
pairs.question: Ex quo Terra, ut ferunt apud Ovidium, novam stirpem in faciem hominum animavit, postquam gigantes montibus obruti sunt?
pairs.question_en: From what, according to the tale in Ovid, did Earth animate a new stock in human shape after the Giants were crushed beneath the mountains?
pairs.answer_en: From the blood of the Giants.
pairs.derivation: The blood-born men: Earth soaks up the Giants' blood and turns it into a violent human race. Anchored to Terra + the Giants; short answer supported verbatim (natorum sanguine ... animasse cruorem ... in faciem vertisse hominum).

pairs.source_text: adfectasse ferunt regnum caeleste gigantas altaque congestos struxisse ad sidera montis. tum pater omnipotens misso perfregit Olympum fulmine et excussit subiecto Pelion Ossae.
pairs.question: Qui, ut ferunt apud Ovidium, regnum caeleste adfectaverunt montibus in altum congestis, donec Iuppiter eos fulmine perfregit?
pairs.question_en: Who, according to the tale in Ovid, aimed at the kingdom of heaven by piling mountains on high, until Jupiter shattered them with his thunderbolt?
pairs.derivation: The Gigantomachy: the Giants pile Pelion on Ossa toward the stars and are struck down by Jove's bolt — canonical shared myth. Anchored to the assault on heaven + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim (gigantas).

pairs.source_text: Est via sublimis, caelo manifesta sereno; lactea nomen habet, candore notabilis ipso. hac iter est superis ad magni tecta Tonantis regalemque domum:
pairs.question: Qua via superi apud Ovidium ad regiam magni Tonantis iter faciunt?
pairs.question_en: By what road, in Ovid, do the gods travel to the royal palace of the great Thunderer?
pairs.derivation: The Milky Way as the road of the gods to Jove's palace — a canonical mythological picture (lactea nomen habet). Anchored to the Thunderer's palace + Ovid; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tertia post illam successit aenea proles, saevior ingeniis et ad horrida promptior arma, non scelerata tamen; de duro est ultima ferro.
pairs.question: Quota inter aetates hominum apud Ovidium fuit aenea proles?
pairs.question_en: Which in order among the ages of mankind in Ovid was the bronze race?
pairs.derivation: The bronze race as third of the four ages (Tertia ... aenea proles) — part of the canonical gold-silver-bronze-iron sequence. Anchored to Ovid's ages; one-word ordinal answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Arcadis hinc sedes et inhospita tecta tyranni ingredior, traherent cum sera crepuscula noctem. signa dedi venisse deum, vulgusque precari coeperat: inridet primo pia vota Lycaon,
pairs.question: Cuius terrae tyrannus erat Lycaon, cuius tecta Iuppiter humana sub imagine intravit?
pairs.question_en: Of what land was Lycaon the tyrant, whose house Jupiter entered in human guise?
pairs.derivation: Lycaon as the Arcadian tyrant (Arcadis ... tecta tyranni) visited by Jove in disguise. Anchored to Lycaon + Jupiter; one-place answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nec contentus eo, missi de gente Molossa obsidis unius iugulum mucrone resolvit atque ita semineces partim ferventibus artus mollit aquis, partim subiecto torruit igni. quod simul inposuit mensis, ego vindice flamma in domino dignos everti tecta penates;
pairs.question: Quales epulas Lycaon Iovi hospiti in mensis apposuit, ut deum experiretur?
pairs.question_en: What sort of feast did Lycaon set on the table before his guest Jupiter, to put the god to the test?
pairs.answer_en: Human flesh — the limbs of a Molossian hostage.
pairs.derivation: Lycaon's crime: he cooks and serves the flesh of a Molossian hostage to test whether his guest is a god. The story every reader knows as the cause of the flood. Anchored to Lycaon + Jove; short answer supported verbatim (obsidis ... artus ... inposuit mensis).

pairs.source_text: in villos abeunt vestes, in crura lacerti: fit lupus et veteris servat vestigia formae; canities eadem est, eadem violentia vultus, idem oculi lucent, eadem feritatis imago est.
pairs.question: In quod animal Lycaon, tyrannus Arcadiae, apud Ovidium mutatus est?
pairs.question_en: Into what animal was Lycaon, the tyrant of Arcadia, transformed in Ovid?
pairs.derivation: The first great transformation of the poem: Lycaon becomes a wolf (fit lupus), keeping traces of his old savagery. Anchored to Lycaon; one-word animal answer verbatim. Canonical myth (and the ambient etymological association with Greek lykos).

pairs.source_text: tela reponuntur manibus fabricata cyclopum; poena placet diversa, genus mortale sub undis perdere et ex omni nimbos demittere caelo.
pairs.question: Qua poena Iuppiter, scelere Lycaonis cognito, genus mortale perdere statuit?
pairs.answer: Diluvio: sub undis nimbisque de caelo demissis.
pairs.question_en: With what punishment did Jupiter, once Lycaon's crime was known, decide to destroy the mortal race?
pairs.answer_en: With a flood: beneath the waters, with storm-clouds sent down from the sky.
pairs.derivation: Jove sets aside the thunderbolt and chooses the flood — the pivot of the whole flood myth (poena placet diversa, genus mortale sub undis perdere). Anchored to Jupiter + Lycaon; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: tela reponuntur manibus fabricata cyclopum;
pairs.question: Quorum manibus fulmina Iovis fabricata esse dicuntur apud Ovidium?
pairs.question_en: By whose hands are Jupiter's thunderbolts said, in Ovid, to have been forged?
pairs.answer_en: By the hands of the Cyclopes.
pairs.derivation: The Cyclopes as forgers of Jove's bolts — a canonical mythological attribute (tela ... fabricata cyclopum). Anchored to Jupiter's weapons; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Protinus Aeoliis Aquilonem claudit in antris et quaecumque fugant inductas flamina nubes emittitque Notum. madidis Notus evolat alis,
pairs.question: Quem ventum Iuppiter emisit, ut nimbis terras diluvio obrueret, Aquilone in antris Aeoliis cluso?
pairs.question_en: Which wind did Jupiter let loose to overwhelm the lands with rain in the flood, after shutting Aquilo in the Aeolian caves?
pairs.derivation: The rain-bringing south wind Notus released (and the cloud-chasing north wind imprisoned) to start the deluge — the winds' canonical characters. Anchored to Jupiter + the flood; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec caelo contenta suo est Iovis ira, sed illum caeruleus frater iuvat auxiliaribus undis.
pairs.question: Quis deus, frater Iovis, iram eius in diluvio auxiliaribus undis iuvit?
pairs.question_en: Which god, Jupiter's brother, aided his wrath in the flood with auxiliary waters?
pairs.derivation: Neptune ('caeruleus frater', the rector pelagi of the following lines) joins the flood with his waters — the standard identification of Jove's sea-god brother. Anchored to Jupiter + the flood; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: Ipse tridente suo terram percussit, at illa intremuit motuque vias patefecit aquarum.
pairs.question: Quo telo Neptunus terram percussit, ut vias aquarum diluvio patefaceret?
pairs.question_en: With what weapon did Neptune strike the earth, to open the ways of the waters for the flood?
pairs.derivation: Neptune strikes the earth with his trident and the waters break out — the god's canonical attribute in action. Anchored to Neptune + the flood; one-word answer verbatim (tridente suo).

pairs.source_text: nec maris ira manet, positoque tricuspide telo mulcet aquas rector pelagi supraque profundum exstantem atque umeros innato murice tectum caeruleum Tritona vocat conchaeque sonanti inspirare iubet fluctusque et flumina signo iam revocare dato:
pairs.question: Quis deus, a rectore pelagi vocatus, concha sonanti fluctus et flumina post diluvium receptui cecinit?
pairs.question_en: Which god, summoned by the ruler of the sea, sounded the retreat for the waves and rivers after the flood on his echoing conch?
pairs.derivation: Triton and his conch-trumpet recall the waters at the end of the flood — the canonical image of the sea-god's herald. Anchored to Neptune (rector pelagi) + the flood's end; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes. hic ubi Deucalion (nam cetera texerat aequor) cum consorte tori parva rate vectus adhaesit,
pairs.question: In quo monte Deucalion cum Pyrrha coniuge, parva rate vectus, post diluvium adhaesit?
pairs.question_en: On what mountain did Deucalion with his wife Pyrrha, borne on a little raft, come to rest after the flood?
pairs.derivation: The sole survivors of the flood land on Parnassus — a core fact of the Deucalion myth. Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha; one-place answer verbatim (nomine Parnasos ... hic ubi Deucalion ... adhaesit).

pairs.source_text: mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes.
pairs.question: Quot verticibus mons Parnasos, ut describit Ovidius, arduus astra petit?
pairs.question_en: With how many peaks does Mount Parnassus, as Ovid describes it, rise steep toward the stars?
pairs.derivation: The twin peaks of Parnassus — a stock geographical fact about the mountain of Apollo and the Muses. Anchored to Parnassus by name; one-number answer verbatim (verticibus ... duobus).

pairs.source_text: Separat Aonios Oetaeis Phocis ab arvis, terra ferax, dum terra fuit, sed tempore in illo pars maris et latus subitarum campus aquarum. mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus, nomine Parnasos, superantque cacumina nubes.
pairs.question: In qua terra situs est mons Parnasos, ubi Deucalion post diluvium adhaesit?
pairs.question_en: In what land is Mount Parnassus situated, where Deucalion came to rest after the flood?
pairs.derivation: Parnassus stands in Phocis, the land between the Aonian (Boeotian) and Oetaean fields — standard Greek geography every reader of the Delphi myths carries. Anchored to Parnassus + Deucalion; one-place answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Corycidas nymphas et numina montis adorant fatidicamque Themin, quae tunc oracla tenebat:
pairs.question: Quae dea fatidica oracula Parnasia tunc tenebat, cum Deucalion et Pyrrha post diluvium eam adirent?
pairs.question_en: Which prophetic goddess then held the oracle at Parnassus, when Deucalion and Pyrrha approached her after the flood?
pairs.derivation: Themis holds the oracle (later Apollo's Delphi) at the time of the flood — a canonical piece of oracle-history (quae tunc oracla tenebat). Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha + Parnassus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Mota dea est sortemque dedit: 'discedite templo et velate caput cinctasque resolvite vestes ossaque post tergum magnae iactate parentis!'
pairs.question: Quid Themis oraculo Deucalioni et Pyrrhae post tergum iactare iussit, ut genus humanum repararetur?
pairs.question_en: What did Themis by her oracle order Deucalion and Pyrrha to throw behind their backs, so that the human race might be restored?
pairs.answer_en: The bones of their great mother.
pairs.derivation: The riddling oracle of Themis — throw the great mother's bones behind you — the hinge of the Deucalion myth. Anchored to Themis + Deucalion + Pyrrha; short answer verbatim (ossaque post tergum magnae iactate parentis).

pairs.source_text: magna parens terra est: lapides in corpore terrae ossa reor dici; iacere hos post terga iubemur.'
pairs.question: Quae esse 'ossa magnae parentis' Deucalion sortem Themidis interpretatus est?
pairs.question_en: What did Deucalion interpret the 'bones of the great mother' in Themis's oracle to be?
pairs.answer_en: The stones in the body of the earth.
pairs.derivation: Deucalion solves the riddle: the great mother is Earth, her bones are stones. The famous interpretation that saves mankind. Anchored to Deucalion + the oracle; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: inque brevi spatio superorum numine saxa missa viri manibus faciem traxere virorum et de femineo reparata est femina iactu.
pairs.question: Post diluvium, de cuius iactu saxa in feminas versa sunt, cum saxa a Deucalione missa virorum faciem traherent?
pairs.question_en: After the flood, from whose throw were the stones turned into women, while the stones cast by Deucalion took on the form of men?
pairs.derivation: The double aetiology: men from the man's stones, women from the woman's (de femineo reparata est femina iactu). Anchored to Deucalion + Pyrrha; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: inde Promethides placidis Epimethida dictis mulcet et 'aut fallax' ait 'est sollertia nobis,
pairs.question: Cuius filius erat Deucalion, qui solus cum coniuge diluvio superfuit?
pairs.question_en: Whose son was Deucalion, who alone with his wife survived the flood?
pairs.derivation: Ovid calls Deucalion 'Promethides' — son of Prometheus — the standard genealogy of the flood-survivor. Anchored to Deucalion; one-name answer supported by the patronymic.

pairs.source_text: inde Promethides placidis Epimethida dictis mulcet et 'aut fallax' ait 'est sollertia nobis,
pairs.question: Cuius filia erat Pyrrha, coniunx Deucalionis?
pairs.question_en: Whose daughter was Pyrrha, the wife of Deucalion?
pairs.derivation: Ovid calls Pyrrha 'Epimethis' — daughter of Epimetheus (brother of Prometheus) — the standard genealogy. Anchored to Pyrrha + Deucalion; one-name answer supported by the patronymic.

pairs.source_text: ergo ubi diluvio tellus lutulenta recenti solibus aetheriis altoque recanduit aestu, edidit innumeras species; partimque figuras rettulit antiquas, partim nova monstra creavit. Illa quidem nollet, sed te quoque, maxime Python, tum genuit, populisque novis, incognita serpens, terror eras:
pairs.question: Unde natus est Python, ingens ille serpens, novorum populorum terror?
pairs.question_en: From what was Python born, that huge serpent, the terror of the new peoples?
pairs.answer_en: From the Earth, after the flood.
pairs.derivation: Python as earth-born from the mud left by the flood — the canonical origin of the Delphic serpent. Anchored to Python by name; short answer supported verbatim (tellus ... te quoque, maxime Python, tum genuit).

pairs.source_text: hunc deus arcitenens, numquam letalibus armis ante nisi in dammis capreisque fugacibus usus, mille gravem telis exhausta paene pharetra perdidit effuso per vulnera nigra veneno.
pairs.question: Quis deus Pythona serpentem mille telis, exhausta paene pharetra, perdidit?
pairs.question_en: Which god destroyed the serpent Python with a thousand arrows, his quiver almost emptied?
pairs.derivation: Apollo's slaying of Python with his arrows — one of the most canonical of all myths, the foundation-story of Delphi. Anchored to Python; one-name answer (deus arcitenens = Apollo, the standard epithet).

pairs.source_text: neve operis famam posset delere vetustas, instituit sacros celebri certamine ludos, Pythia de domitae serpentis nomine dictos.
pairs.question: Quos ludos sacros Apollo instituit, ne fama Pythonis domiti vetustate deleretur?
pairs.answer: Ludos Pythios, de nomine serpentis dictos.
pairs.question_en: What sacred games did Apollo found, so that the fame of his conquest of Python should not fade with time?
pairs.answer_en: The Pythian games, named after the serpent.
pairs.derivation: The aetiology of the Pythian games: founded by Apollo as a memorial of the slain serpent and named for it (Pythia de domitae serpentis nomine dictos). Anchored to Apollo + Python; short answer verbatim. A cult fact of the shared Greco-Roman calendar of games.

pairs.source_text: hic iuvenum quicumque manu pedibusve rotave vicerat, aesculeae capiebat frondis honorem. nondum laurus erat, longoque decentia crine tempora cingebat de qualibet arbore Phoebus.
pairs.question: Cuius arboris fronde victores ludorum Pythiorum primo coronabantur, cum laurus nondum esset?
pairs.question_en: With the foliage of what tree were the victors of the Pythian games first crowned, when the laurel did not yet exist?
pairs.derivation: Before Daphne became the laurel, the Pythian prize was oak foliage (aesculeae frondis honorem; nondum laurus erat) — the detail that sets up the Daphne aetiology. Anchored to the Pythian games; one-word tree answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia, quem non fors ignara dedit, sed saeva Cupidinis ira,
pairs.question: Quis fuit primus amor Phoebi, ut narrat Ovidius in primo Metamorphoseon libro?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first love of Phoebus, as Ovid tells in the first book of the Metamorphoses?
pairs.derivation: The programmatic opening of the Daphne episode: 'Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia.' Anchored to Phoebus + Ovid; one-name answer verbatim. The centerpiece myth of the book.

pairs.source_text: Primus amor Phoebi Daphne Peneia, quem non fors ignara dedit, sed saeva Cupidinis ira,
pairs.question: Cuius dei saeva ira, non fors, amorem Phoebi in Daphnen excitavit?
pairs.question_en: Whose fierce divine anger — not chance — kindled Phoebus's love for Daphne?
pairs.derivation: The cause of the whole episode: not blind chance but the wrath of Cupid, whom Apollo had mocked after slaying Python. Anchored to Phoebus + Daphne; one-name answer verbatim (saeva Cupidinis ira).

pairs.source_text: dixit et eliso percussis aere pennis inpiger umbrosa Parnasi constitit arce
pairs.question: In cuius montis arce Cupido constitit, cum tela sua in Phoebum Daphnenque directurus esset?
pairs.question_en: On the summit of what mountain did Cupid take his stand, when about to aim his arrows at Phoebus and Daphne?
pairs.derivation: Cupid shoots his two arrows from the shady citadel of Parnassus — the staging of the Daphne myth. Anchored to Cupid + Phoebus + Daphne; one-place answer verbatim (umbrosa Parnasi ... arce).

pairs.source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
pairs.question: Ex quo metallo factum erat telum Cupidinis quod amorem facit?
pairs.question_en: Of what metal was Cupid's arrow made that causes love?
pairs.derivation: Cupid's two arrows of opposite powers: the love-making one is golden and sharp. One of the most famous images in Latin poetry. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (quod facit, auratum est).

pairs.source_text: eque sagittifera prompsit duo tela pharetra diversorum operum: fugat hoc, facit illud amorem; quod facit, auratum est et cuspide fulget acuta, quod fugat, obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum.
pairs.question: Quod metallum habet sub harundine telum Cupidinis quod amorem fugat?
pairs.question_en: What metal does Cupid's arrow that puts love to flight carry beneath its shaft?
pairs.derivation: The counterpart arrow: blunt and leaden, it repels love. Anchored to Cupid's arrows; one-word metal answer verbatim (obtusum est et habet sub harundine plumbum).

pairs.source_text: hoc deus in nympha Peneide fixit, at illo laesit Apollineas traiecta per ossa medullas;
pairs.question: Utrum telum, plumbeumne an auratum, Cupido in Daphnen nympham Peneida fixit?
pairs.question_en: Which arrow, the leaden or the golden, did Cupid plant in Daphne, the nymph daughter of Peneus?
pairs.answer_en: The leaden one, which puts love to flight.
pairs.derivation: The mechanism of the myth: the lead (love-fleeing) arrow strikes Daphne, the gold one pierces Apollo — hence pursuit and flight. Anchored to Cupid + Daphne; short answer supported verbatim (hoc = quod fugat, in nympha Peneide fixit).

pairs.source_text: 'da mihi perpetua, genitor carissime,' dixit 'virginitate frui! dedit hoc pater ante Dianae.'
pairs.question: Quid Daphne a genitore suo Peneo petivit, exemplum Dianae secuta?
pairs.question_en: What did Daphne ask of her father Peneus, following the example of Diana?
pairs.derivation: Daphne's wish for perpetual virginity like Diana's, granted (in word) by her father — a core element of the myth (dedit hoc pater ante Dianae; cf. innuptaeque aemula Phoebes, 1.476). Anchored to Daphne + Peneus + Diana; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: mihi Delphica tellus et Claros et Tenedos Patareaque regia servit; Iuppiter est genitor;
pairs.question: Cui deo serviunt Delphica tellus et Claros et Tenedos Patareaque regia, ut ipse apud Ovidium gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: Which god do the Delphic land, Claros, Tenedos, and the royal seat of Patara serve, as he himself boasts in Ovid?
pairs.derivation: Apollo's canonical oracle-seats, listed by the god himself in his plea to Daphne (the speaker, son of Jupiter, is Phoebus). Anchored by the four named cult places; one-name answer. Shared religious geography of the Apollo cult.

pairs.source_text: inventum medicina meum est, opiferque per orbem dicor, et herbarum subiecta potentia nobis.
pairs.question: Cuius dei inventum medicina est, qui 'opifer' per orbem dicitur, ut apud Ovidium legimus?
pairs.question_en: Which god's invention is medicine — the god called 'help-bringer' throughout the world, as we read in Ovid?
pairs.derivation: Apollo as inventor of medicine and lord of herbs, with the cult epithet 'opifer' — spoken by the god himself in the Daphne episode. A canonical divine attribute; one-name answer. Anchored by the epithet + the invention of medicine.

pairs.source_text: viribus absumptis expalluit illa citaeque victa labore fugae spectans Peneidas undas 'fer, pater,' inquit 'opem! si flumina numen habetis, qua nimium placui, mutando perde figuram!'
pairs.question: Quem Daphne, victa labore fugae, oravit ut opem ferret figuramque suam mutando perderet?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Daphne, overcome by the effort of her flight, beg to bring help and destroy her beauty by changing it?
pairs.derivation: Daphne's prayer at the climax of the chase, addressed to her father the river ('fer, pater... opem', gazing at the Peneian waters) — the prayer that triggers the transformation. Anchored to Daphne; short answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cui deus 'at, quoniam coniunx mea non potes esse, arbor eris certe' dixit 'mea! semper habebunt te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae;
pairs.question: In quam arborem Daphne, Penei filia, Apollinem fugiens mutata est?
pairs.question_en: Into what tree was Daphne, the daughter of Peneus, transformed as she fled Apollo?
pairs.derivation: THE central fact of the episode: Daphne becomes the laurel — Apollo addresses the new tree as 'laure'. The paradigm 'who was turned into what' cultural fact (cited in issue #2 itself). Anchored to Daphne + Apollo; one-word tree answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cui deus 'at, quoniam coniunx mea non potes esse, arbor eris certe' dixit 'mea! semper habebunt te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae;
pairs.question: Quae tria Apollinis laurum semper habitura esse deus ipse Daphnae in arborem mutatae promisit?
pairs.question_en: What three things of Apollo's did the god himself promise would always bear the laurel, when Daphne had been changed into the tree?
pairs.answer_en: His hair, his lyres, and his quivers.
pairs.derivation: Apollo's adoption of the laurel for his hair, lyre, and quiver — the aetiology of the god's most familiar attribute. Anchored to Apollo + the laurel; brief three-item answer verbatim (te coma, te citharae, te nostrae, laure, pharetrae).

pairs.source_text: tu ducibus Latiis aderis, cum laeta Triumphum vox canet et visent longas Capitolia pompas;
pairs.question: Quae arbor ducibus Latiis in triumphis adest, cum laeta vox Triumphum canit et Capitolia longas pompas visunt?
pairs.question_en: What tree attends Latin generals in their triumphs, when the joyful voice sings 'Triumphus' and the Capitol beholds the long processions?
pairs.derivation: The laurel of the Roman triumph, prophesied by Apollo to the new-made tree — the prime culture-fact linking the Daphne myth to Roman civic religion. Anchored to the triumph + the Capitol; one-word answer (the addressee is the laurel of 1.559).

pairs.source_text: postibus Augustis eadem fidissima custos ante fores stabis mediamque tuebere quercum,
pairs.question: Ante cuius fores laurus, ut Apollo apud Ovidium praedixit, fidissima custos stat?
pairs.question_en: Before whose doors, as Apollo foretold in Ovid, does the laurel stand as most faithful guardian?
pairs.derivation: The laurels flanking Augustus' doorposts (postibus Augustis) — a celebrated honor of 27 BC, woven by Ovid into the Daphne aetiology. Anchored to the laurel + Augustus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: postibus Augustis eadem fidissima custos ante fores stabis mediamque tuebere quercum,
pairs.question: Quam arborem mediam laurus ante fores Augusti custodit, ut Apollo praedixit?
pairs.question_en: What tree in the middle does the laurel guard before the doors of Augustus, as Apollo foretold?
pairs.derivation: The oak wreath (corona civica, 'ob cives servatos') over Augustus' door, flanked by the laurels — the paired honors of 27 BC known to every Roman. Anchored to Augustus' doors + the laurel; one-word answer verbatim (mediam ... quercum).

pairs.source_text: utque meum intonsis caput est iuvenale capillis, tu quoque perpetuos semper gere frondis honores!'
pairs.question: Quales frondis honores laurus, Apolline iubente, semper gerit, sicut caput dei intonsis capillis iuvenale est?
pairs.question_en: What kind of honors of foliage does the laurel always wear, at Apollo's command, just as the god's head is youthful with unshorn hair?
pairs.derivation: The aetiology of the evergreen laurel: Apollo grants it perpetual foliage matching his own unshorn, ever-young hair. Anchored to Apollo + the laurel; short answer verbatim (perpetuos semper gere frondis honores).

pairs.source_text: Est nemus Haemoniae, praerupta quod undique claudit silva: vocant Tempe; per quae Peneos ab imo effusus Pindo spumosis volvitur undis
pairs.question: Quod nemus Haemoniae, silva praerupta undique clausum, Peneos amnis perfluit?
pairs.question_en: What grove of Haemonia (Thessaly), shut in on every side by steep forest, does the river Peneus flow through?
pairs.derivation: The vale of Tempe in Thessaly, through which the Peneus flows — proverbial beauty-spot of ancient geography (vocant Tempe). Anchored to Haemonia + the Peneus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Est nemus Haemoniae, praerupta quod undique claudit silva: vocant Tempe; per quae Peneos ab imo effusus Pindo spumosis volvitur undis
pairs.question: Ex quo monte effusus Peneos amnis per Tempe spumosis undis volvitur?
pairs.question_en: From what mountain does the river Peneus pour forth and roll through Tempe with foaming waters?
pairs.derivation: The Peneus rises from Mount Pindus and flows through Tempe — standard Thessalian geography carried by every reader of the poets. Anchored to the Peneus + Tempe; one-place answer verbatim (ab imo effusus Pindo).

pairs.source_text: Inachus unus abest imoque reconditus antro fletibus auget aquas natamque miserrimus Io luget ut amissam:
pairs.question: Cuius amnis filia erat Io, quam Iuppiter amavit?
pairs.question_en: Of what river was Io, whom Jupiter loved, the daughter?
pairs.derivation: Io as daughter of the Argive river-god Inachus (natam ... Io) — the canonical genealogy that opens the episode. Anchored to Io + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: cum deus inducta latas caligine terras occuluit tenuitque fugam rapuitque pudorem.
pairs.question: Qua re inducta Iuppiter terras occuluit, cum Io fugientem comprehendit?
pairs.question_en: By spreading what did Jupiter hide the lands, when he caught the fleeing Io?
pairs.derivation: Jove's covering cloud — the sudden darkness over Argos that Juno immediately notices — the signature device of the Io story. Anchored to Jupiter + Io; one-word answer verbatim (inducta ... caligine).

pairs.source_text: coniugis adventum praesenserat inque nitentem Inachidos vultus mutaverat ille iuvencam;
pairs.question: In quod animal Iuppiter Io, Inachi filiam, mutavit, cum adventum Iunonis praesensisset?
pairs.question_en: Into what animal did Jupiter change Io, the daughter of Inachus, when he had sensed Juno's approach?
pairs.derivation: The central transformation of the Io myth: Jupiter himself turns her into a shining heifer to hide his affair from Juno. Anchored to Io + Jupiter + Juno; one-word animal answer verbatim (nitentem ... iuvencam).

pairs.source_text: Iuppiter e terra genitam mentitur, ut auctor desinat inquiri: petit hanc Saturnia munus.
pairs.question: Quod munus Iuno Saturnia a Iove petivit, cum Io in vaccam formosam mutata esset?
pairs.question_en: What gift did Saturnian Juno demand of Jupiter, when Io had been changed into a beautiful cow?
pairs.derivation: Juno's cunning counter-move: she asks for the heifer as a present, and Jove cannot refuse without betraying himself. Anchored to Juno + Jupiter + the transformed Io; short answer verbatim (petit hanc Saturnia munus).

pairs.source_text: Paelice donata non protinus exuit omnem diva metum timuitque Iovem et fuit anxia furti, donec Arestoridae servandam tradidit Argo.
pairs.question: Cui custodi Iuno vaccam Io servandam tradidit?
pairs.question_en: To what guardian did Juno hand over the cow Io to be kept?
pairs.derivation: Juno entrusts Io to Argus (the patronymic Arestorides gives his father Arestor) — the watchman of the canonical tale. Anchored to Juno + Io; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: centum luminibus cinctum caput Argus habebat inde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem, cetera servabant atque in statione manebant.
pairs.question: Quot luminibus cinctum caput habebat Argus, custos Ius a Iunone datus?
pairs.question_en: With how many eyes was the head of Argus ringed, the guard set over Io by Juno?
pairs.derivation: The hundred eyes of Argus — his defining canonical attribute (centum luminibus cinctum caput). Anchored to Argus + Io; one-number answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: centum luminibus cinctum caput Argus habebat inde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem, cetera servabant atque in statione manebant.
pairs.question: Quot oculi Argi centoculi suis vicibus simul quietem capiebant, ceteris in statione manentibus?
pairs.question_en: How many of hundred-eyed Argus's eyes took their rest at a time in turn, while the rest stayed on watch?
pairs.derivation: The famous detail that only two of Argus's hundred eyes slept at a time, the rest keeping watch — why he was the perfect guard. Anchored to Argus; one-number answer verbatim (capiebant bina quietem).

pairs.source_text: littera pro verbis, quam pes in pulvere duxit, corporis indicium mutati triste peregit.
pairs.question: Quo modo Io in vaccam mutata patri Inacho, quae esset, indicavit?
pairs.question_en: How did Io, changed into a cow, reveal to her father Inachus who she was?
pairs.answer_en: By letters traced in the dust with her hoof.
pairs.derivation: The pathetic recognition scene: mute Io writes her name in the dust with her hoof (littera ... quam pes in pulvere duxit). A celebrated moment of the myth. Anchored to Io + Inachus; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec superum rector mala tanta Phoronidos ultra ferre potest natumque vocat, quem lucida partu Pleias enixa est letoque det imperat Argum.
pairs.question: Quem filium Iuppiter vocavit, cum imperaret ut Argus, custos Ius, leto daretur?
pairs.question_en: Which son did Jupiter summon, when he ordered that Argus, Io's guard, be put to death?
pairs.derivation: Jove sends Mercury — 'the son whom the bright Pleiad bore' (Maia) — to kill Argus. The identification of the Pleiad's son as Mercury is canonical shared knowledge. Anchored to Jupiter + Argus + Io; one-name answer.

pairs.source_text: parva mora est alas pedibus virgamque potenti somniferam sumpsisse manu tegumenque capillis.
pairs.question: Quae tria Mercurius sumpsit, ad Argum necandum a Iove missus?
pairs.answer: Alas pedibus, virgam somniferam, tegumen capillis.
pairs.question_en: What three things did Mercury take up, when sent by Jupiter to kill Argus?
pairs.answer_en: Wings for his feet, the sleep-bringing wand, and the cap for his hair.
pairs.derivation: Mercury's canonical kit — the winged sandals (talaria), the sleep-bringing wand (caduceus/virga somnifera), and the traveler's cap (petasus) — assumed for the Argus mission. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; brief three-item answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: parte tamen vigilat. quaerit quoque (namque reperta fistula nuper erat), qua sit ratione reperta. Tum deus 'Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus' inquit 'inter hamadryadas celeberrima Nonacrinas naias una fuit: nymphae Syringa vocabant.
pairs.question: De qua nympha Mercurius Argo fabulam narrare coepit, ut servantia lumina somno evinceret?
pairs.question_en: About which nymph did Mercury begin to tell Argus a tale, in order to overcome his watching eyes with sleep?
pairs.derivation: The tale-within-the-tale: Mercury lulls Argus with the story of Pan and Syrinx, prompted by Argus's question about the newly invented pipe. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; one-name answer verbatim (nymphae Syringa vocabant).

pairs.source_text: Tum deus 'Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus' inquit 'inter hamadryadas celeberrima Nonacrinas naias una fuit: nymphae Syringa vocabant.
pairs.question: Cuius terrae nympha erat Syrinx, inter hamadryadas Nonacrinas celeberrima naias?
pairs.question_en: Of what land was Syrinx a nymph, the most famous naiad among the Nonacrian hamadryads?
pairs.derivation: Syrinx as an Arcadian naiad (from Nonacris, under Arcadia's cold mountains), a devotee of Diana like Daphne. Anchored to Syrinx by name; one-place answer verbatim (Arcadiae gelidis sub montibus).

pairs.source_text: et precibus spretis fugisse per avia nympham, donec harenosi placidum Ladonis ad amnem venerit;
pairs.question: Ad quem amnem Syrinx nympha, Pana et preces eius fugiens, tandem pervenit?
pairs.question_en: To what river did the nymph Syrinx at last come, fleeing Pan and his entreaties?
pairs.derivation: The sandy Ladon (an Arcadian river) halts Syrinx's flight — the setting of her transformation. Anchored to Syrinx + Pan; one-name river answer verbatim (harenosi ... Ladonis ad amnem).

pairs.source_text: hic illam cursum inpedientibus undis ut se mutarent liquidas orasse sorores, Panaque cum prensam sibi iam Syringa putaret, corpore pro nymphae calamos tenuisse palustres,
pairs.question: In quas res Syrinx mutata est, cum Pan eam iam prensam se tenere putaret?
pairs.question_en: Into what was Syrinx changed, when Pan thought he already held her in his grasp?
pairs.derivation: The transformation at the heart of the panpipe aetiology: Pan grasps reeds instead of the nymph (corpore pro nymphae calamos ... palustres). Anchored to Syrinx + Pan; short answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: atque ita disparibus calamis conpagine cerae inter se iunctis nomen tenuisse puellae.
pairs.question: Cuius puellae nomen tenet fistula, quam Pan disparibus calamis cera inter se iunctis composuit?
pairs.question_en: Whose name does the pipe keep, which Pan made of unequal reeds joined together with wax?
pairs.derivation: The aetiology of the panpipes (syrinx/fistula): unequal reeds bound with wax, keeping the name of the girl. A canonical culture-fact about the shepherd's instrument. Anchored to Pan + the pipe; one-name answer verbatim (nomen tenuisse puellae).

pairs.source_text: talia dicturus vidit Cyllenius omnes subcubuisse oculos adopertaque lumina somno; supprimit extemplo vocem firmatque soporem languida permulcens medicata lumina virga. nec mora, falcato nutantem vulnerat ense, qua collo est confine caput, saxoque cruentum deicit et maculat praeruptam sanguine rupem.
pairs.question: Quis deus Argum centoculum, omnibus oculis somno victis, occidit?
pairs.question_en: Which god killed hundred-eyed Argus, when all his eyes had been overcome by sleep?
pairs.derivation: Mercury (Cyllenius, from his birthplace Mount Cyllene) beheads the sleeping Argus — the resolution of the watchman tale, hence his epithet Argiphontes. Anchored to Argus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: nec mora, falcato nutantem vulnerat ense, qua collo est confine caput,
pairs.question: Quali ense Mercurius Argum nutantem vulneravit, qua collo caput confine est?
pairs.question_en: With what kind of sword did Mercury strike the nodding Argus, where the head borders on the neck?
pairs.derivation: The falcatus ensis — the curved harpe of Mercury (the same blade type Perseus later wields) — used to behead Argus. Anchored to Mercury + Argus; one-word answer verbatim (falcato ... ense).

pairs.source_text: Excipit hos volucrisque suae Saturnia pennis collocat et gemmis caudam stellantibus inplet.
pairs.question: In cuius avis pennis Iuno centum oculos Argi occisi collocavit?
pairs.question_en: On the feathers of what bird did Juno place the hundred eyes of the slain Argus?
pairs.answer_en: On the feathers of the peacock, her own bird.
pairs.derivation: The aetiology of the peacock's starry tail: Juno sets Argus's eyes on the feathers of 'her bird' — the peacock, Juno's canonical bird. Anchored to Juno + Argus; the identification volucris sua = pavo is the shared knowledge the question tests.

pairs.source_text: protinus exarsit nec tempora distulit irae horriferamque oculis animoque obiecit Erinyn paelicis Argolicae stimulosque in pectore caecos condidit et profugam per totum exercuit orbem.
pairs.question: Quam ultricem Iuno, Argo occiso, oculis animoque Ius obiecit, ut eam profugam per totum orbem ageret?
pairs.question_en: What avenging spirit did Juno, after Argus was killed, set before the eyes and mind of Io, to drive her as a fugitive over the whole world?
pairs.derivation: In Ovid's version Juno torments Io with a horrifying Erinys and blind goads, driving her across the world (the gadfly of the Greek tradition). Anchored to Juno + Io; one-name answer verbatim (obiecit Erinyn).

pairs.source_text: ultimus inmenso restabas, Nile, labori; quem simulac tetigit, positisque in margine ripae procubuit genibus resupinoque ardua collo,
pairs.question: Quod flumen ultimum inmenso labori Ius profugae restabat?
pairs.question_en: What river remained as the last stage of the fugitive Io's immense toil?
pairs.derivation: Io's wanderings end at the Nile — the canonical link of the Argive heifer to Egypt, where she becomes a goddess. Anchored to Io; one-name river answer verbatim (ultimus ... restabas, Nile, labori).

pairs.source_text: finiat ut poenas tandem, rogat 'in' que 'futurum pone metus' inquit: 'numquam tibi causa doloris haec erit,' et Stygias iubet hoc audire paludes.
pairs.question: Quas paludes Iuppiter audire iussit, cum Iunoni promitteret Io numquam posthac causam doloris futuram esse?
pairs.question_en: What waters did Jupiter order to hear his words, when he promised Juno that Io would never again be a cause of grief?
pairs.derivation: Jove seals his promise by calling the Stygian waters to witness — the inviolable oath of the gods by the Styx, a canonical piece of divine custom. Anchored to Jupiter + Juno + Io; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ut lenita dea est, vultus capit illa priores fitque, quod ante fuit: fugiunt e corpore saetae, cornua decrescunt, fit luminis artior orbis, contrahitur rictus, redeunt umerique manusque, ungulaque in quinos dilapsa absumitur ungues: de bove nil superest formae nisi candor in illa.
pairs.question: Quid unum de bove in Io, formae pristinae redditae, superfuit?
pairs.question_en: What single trace of the cow remained in Io, when she was restored to her former shape?
pairs.derivation: Io's restoration once Juno is appeased: everything bovine vanishes except her radiant whiteness (de bove nil superest formae nisi candor). Anchored to Io; one-word answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nunc dea linigera colitur celeberrima turba.
pairs.question: A quali turba Io, dea facta, nunc celeberrima colitur, ut Ovidius scribit?
pairs.question_en: By what sort of throng is Io, now made a goddess, worshipped most famously, as Ovid writes?
pairs.answer_en: By the linen-wearing throng (the Egyptian worshippers of Isis).
pairs.derivation: Io restored and worshipped as a goddess by the linen-clad crowd — the linen-wearing (linigera) devotees mark the Egyptian cult of Isis, with whom Io was identified. Anchored to Io + her deification; short answer verbatim. A cult fact of shared Greco-Roman religion.

pairs.source_text: huic Epaphus magni genitus de semine tandem creditur esse Iovis perque urbes iuncta parenti templa tenet.
pairs.question: Quis filius Ius de semine magni Iovis genitus esse creditur, qui per urbes templa iuncta matri tenet?
pairs.question_en: Which son of Io is believed to have been begotten of great Jupiter's seed, holding temples in the cities joined to his mother's?
pairs.derivation: Epaphus, son of Io by Jove, worshipped in temples beside his mother's — the genealogical bridge to the Phaethon story. Anchored to Io + Jupiter; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: fuit huic animis aequalis et annis Sole satus Phaethon, quem quondam magna loquentem nec sibi cedentem Phoeboque parente superbum
pairs.question: Quo patre satus esse ferebatur Phaethon, Epapho animis annisque aequalis?
pairs.question_en: Of what father was Phaethon, the equal of Epaphus in spirit and years, said to be born?
pairs.derivation: Phaethon as son of the Sun (Sole satus), proud of his father Phoebus — the premise of the story that spills into book 2. Anchored to Phaethon + Epaphus; one-name answer verbatim.

pairs.source_text: quem quondam magna loquentem nec sibi cedentem Phoeboque parente superbum non tulit Inachides 'matri' que ait 'omnia demens credis et es tumidus genitoris imagine falsi.'
pairs.question: Quis Phaethonti, Phoebo parente superbo, obiecit eum imagine falsi genitoris tumidum esse?
pairs.question_en: Who taunted Phaethon, proud of his father Phoebus, that he was puffed up with the image of a false father?
pairs.derivation: The taunt of Epaphus (called Inachides, grandson of Inachus through Io) that sets Phaethon on his fatal quest. Anchored to Phaethon + Phoebus; one-name answer supported verbatim.

pairs.source_text: erubuit Phaethon iramque pudore repressit et tulit ad Clymenen Epaphi convicia matrem
pairs.question: Quae erat mater Phaethontis, ad quam convicia Epaphi rettulit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the mother of Phaethon, to whom he carried back the insults of Epaphus?
pairs.derivation: Clymene as Phaethon's mother, to whom the boy brings Epaphus's taunt and who swears by the Sun that the Sun is his father. Anchored to Phaethon + Epaphus; one-name answer verbatim (ad Clymenen ... matrem).

pairs.source_text: emicat extemplo laetus post talia matris dicta suae Phaethon et concipit aethera mente Aethiopasque suos positosque sub ignibus Indos sidereis transit patriosque adit inpiger ortus.
pairs.question: Quas gentes Phaethon transiit, cum ad patrios Solis ortus profectus esset?
pairs.question_en: What peoples did Phaethon pass through, when he set out for the rising-place of his father the Sun?
pairs.derivation: The close of book 1: Phaethon crosses his Ethiopians and the Indians beneath the starry fires to reach his father's rising-place (the palace of the Sun, where book 2 opens). Anchored to Phaethon + the Sun; brief two-name answer verbatim.
